*Al-kabad* (with two fathahs) is toil and hardship. The exegetes have multiplied their statements on the intended meaning of *kabad*, but none of them paid attention to linking the relevance between what they explain *kabad* by and the context of the discourse, and its opening with an oath which signals emphasis and the expectation of denial, so much so that they seem to be explaining a single isolated word which does not occur within a speech that must be coherent and harmonious.

They have also overlooked the placement of the verb *khalaqnā* ("We created") in their explanation of *kabad*, for then the verb *khalaqnā* would function as an excuse for the disbelieving man in his being constantly accompanied by *kabad*, since he is created within it, and this would reduce the severity of the rebuke and blame. The arrangement of this preface is like the preface in His words ﴿We have certainly created man in the best of stature, then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ [al-Tin: 4], after the oath ﴿By the fig and the olive﴾ [al-Tin: 1], and so on.

The meaning of (﴿Does he think that none will have power over him?﴾ [Al-Balad: 5]) is: Does he think that We will not have power over him after his body has decayed, so that We would return him to a different creation? This is in the same manner as the oath and the sworn matter in His saying, exalted is He: (﴿I swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Al-Qiyamah: 1]) up to His saying: (﴿Does man think that We will not gather his bones?﴾ [Al-Qiyamah: 3] ﴿Yes, [We are] able to put together even his fingertips﴾ [Al-Qiyamah: 4]). That is: just as We created him the first time in toil through the stages of life, so We will create him a second creation in hardship (kabad) of torment in the Hereafter, because of his disbelief.

By this, the placement of the insertion (idmaj) of His saying, "in hardship," becomes clear, because the intended purpose is the comparison (tanzir) between the first and second creations in that both are within the power of God, exalted is He.

The sense of place (zarfiyyah) in His saying, "in hardship," is used figuratively to mean constant accompaniment (mulazamah), as if he were contained within hardship. Its parallel is His saying: (﴿Rather, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are in torment and far error﴾ [Saba': 8] ﴿Have they not looked at what is before them and what is behind them?﴾ [Saba': 9]) and so on. So what is meant is the torment of this world, which is the hardship of agitation of mind in denial, the fabrication of excuses, and bewilderment about the matter, according to one of the two interpretations of that verse.

So the meaning is that hardship (kabad) is constantly accompanying the polytheist from the time he is characterized by association (shirk), which is the time the intellect becomes upright and perception is complete.

It is also permissible to regard His saying, "Indeed, We created man in hardship," as an inversion (qalb) that is accepted, because it implies a subtle consideration, namely the intensity of hardship's attachment to the polytheist human, to the extent that it is as though he was created in hardship.

The meaning is: We created hardship within the disbelieving human.

The commentators have other interpretations of the meaning of the verse, which the context does not support.

God, exalted, said: ﴿And when Abraham said: My Lord, make this city secure, and keep me and my sons far from worshipping idols﴾ [Ibrahim: 35]. Then He said: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in an uncultivated valley beside Your sacred house﴾ [Ibrahim: 37]. Abraham is the begetter of the original inhabitants of that city. God, exalted, said: ﴿the religion of your father Abraham﴾ [al-Hajj: 78]. And because he is the begetter of Muhammad ﷺ.

*Mā walada* is a relative pronoun with its clause, and the hidden pronoun in *walada* refers back to *wālid*. The meaning is: and what Abraham begot of sons and offspring. This is restricted to those who followed his guidance, and so it includes Muhammad ﷺ.

In this there is an allusion (*ta'rīḍ*) that directs attention to the polytheists among the descendants of Abraham: that they have deviated from the way of their father, which was monotheism, righteousness, calling to the truth, and maintaining the Sacred Mosque. God, exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, the people most worthy of Abraham are those who followed him, and this Prophet and those who believe﴾ [Al 'Imran: 68].

The relative pronoun *mā* is used in His words *wa-mā walada* ("and what he begot") rather than *man* ("who"), although *man* is more commonly used for rational beings, and rational beings are intended here. *Mā* is used instead of *man* because *mā* is more indefinite, so the intent is to magnify the people of this clause, and for the purpose of magnification the most indefinite relative pronoun is used for them. A parallel is His, exalted, statement: ﴿And God knows best what she had given birth to﴾ [Al 'Imran: 36], meaning: a child of wondrous state. What clarifies this is that *mā* is used as an indefinite complete form (*nakira tāmmah*) by general agreement, whereas *man* is used in this way only according to al-Fārisī.

[Page 350]

Also, because the strength of indefiniteness in *mā* is more suited to the intention of a group rather than one specific individual. Do you not see the verse of al-Hakam al-Asamm al-Fazari:

*Meanness is more noble than Wabr and his begetter,*
*and meanness is more noble than Wabr and what the two begot.*

He means: and of his offspring, not one specific child.

The clause ﴿We have certainly created man in toil﴾ is the answer to the oath, and it is the purpose of the surah.

*Al-insān* ("man") may be intended as a genus, and this is the more apparent reading and the view of the majority of the exegetes. Then the definite article is a definition of the genus. What is then intended is specifically the people of association (*shirk*), because His words ﴿Does he think that no one will ever have power over him?﴾ [al-Balad: 5], up to the end of the verses, befit only the states of those who are not believers. The generality is a customary generality, that is, "man" in the custom of people at that time, when the Muslims were only a small group. For this reason the Qur'an frequently uses "man" to mean the disbelievers among people.

It may also be that *al-insān* refers to a specific individual, and then the definite article is the definition of familiarity (*ta'rīf al-'ahd*). On the authority of al-Kalbi, he is Abu al-Ashudd, also called Abu al-Ashaddayn, whose name was Usayd ibn Kaladah al-Jumahi, who was known for strength and force. He would place a leather hide of 'Ukaz beneath his feet and say: "Whoever moves me from here will receive such-and-such." Ten men would pull him, until the hide was torn and his feet did not move. He was extremely hostile to disbelief and enmity toward the Prophet ﷺ, and so ﴿Does he think that no one will ever have power over him?﴾ was revealed concerning him. It is also said that he is al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, and it is said that he is Abu Jahl. From Muqatil: it was revealed concerning al-Harith ibn 'Amir ibn Nawfal, who claimed that he had spent money to corrupt the affair of the Prophet ﷺ. It is also said that he is 'Amr ibn 'Abd Wudd, who charged into the trench on the day of the Confederates to enter Madinah, and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib killed him behind the trench.

These statements have no support from sound transmission, and neither the oath nor the context suits them.

*Al-khalq* ("creation") is bringing into existence what did not exist. It is also applied to the bringing about of a state that has a strong effect on the essence, as in His words: ﴿He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation﴾ [al-Zumar: 6], and His words: ﴿when you shape from clay something like the form of a bird﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 110]. So it is a making that changes the essence of a thing.

[Page 351]

*Al-kabad* (with two fathahs) is toil and hardship. The exegetes have multiplied their statements on the intended meaning of *kabad*, but none of them paid attention to linking the relevance between what they explain *kabad* by and the context of the discourse, and its opening with an oath which signals emphasis and the expectation of denial, so much so that they seem to be explaining a single isolated word which does not occur within a speech that must be coherent and harmonious.

They have also overlooked the placement of the verb *khalaqnā* ("We created") in their explanation of *kabad*, for then the verb *khalaqnā* would function as an excuse for the disbelieving man in his being constantly accompanied by *kabad*, since he is created within it, and this would reduce the severity of the rebuke and blame. So what agrees with the context and suits the oath is that *kabad* is the toil that accompanies the people of association from their belief in a plurality of gods, and the confusion of their opinion in combining the claim of partners for God, exalted, with their turning to God in seeking provision and seeking deliverance when harm befalls them, and from their denial of resurrection after death although they acknowledge the first creation. Therefore His words ﴿We have certainly created man in toil﴾ are not intended in themselves alone, but are a preparation for His words ﴿Does he think that no one will ever have power over him?﴾ [al-Balad: 5]. The intended meaning is the proof of the re-creation of man after death for resurrection and recompense, which they denied, and which the Qur'an began to establish in many of the early surahs.

The arrangement of this preface is like the preface in His words ﴿We have certainly created man in the best of stature, then We returned him to the lowest of the low﴾ [al-Tin: 4], after the oath ﴿By the fig and the olive﴾ [al-Tin: 1], and so on.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 90, verse 1–4 (part 2 of 2):

The meaning of (﴿Does he think that none will have power over him?﴾ [Al-Balad: 5]) is: Does he think that We will not have power over him after his body has decayed, so that We would return him to a different creation? This is in the same manner as the oath and the sworn matter in His saying, exalted is He: (﴿I swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Al-Qiyamah: 1]) up to His saying: (﴿Does man think that We will not gather his bones?﴾ [Al-Qiyamah: 3] ﴿Yes, [We are] able to put together even his fingertips﴾ [Al-Qiyamah: 4]). That is: just as We created him the first time in toil through the stages of life, so We will create him a second creation in hardship (kabad) of torment in the Hereafter, because of his disbelief.

By this, the placement of the insertion (idmaj) of His saying, "in hardship," becomes clear, because the intended purpose is the comparison (tanzir) between the first and second creations in that both are within the power of God, exalted is He.

The sense of place (zarfiyyah) in His saying, "in hardship," is used figuratively to mean constant accompaniment (mulazamah), as if he were contained within hardship. Its parallel is His saying: (﴿Rather, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are in torment and far error﴾ [Saba': 8] ﴿Have they not looked at what is before them and what is behind them?﴾ [Saba': 9]) and so on. So what is meant is the torment of this world, which is the hardship of agitation of mind in denial, the fabrication of excuses, and bewilderment about the matter, according to one of the two interpretations of that verse.

So the meaning is that hardship (kabad) is constantly accompanying the polytheist from the time he is characterized by association (shirk), which is the time the intellect becomes upright and perception is complete.

It is also permissible to regard His saying, "Indeed, We created man in hardship," as an inversion (qalb) that is accepted, because it implies a subtle consideration, namely the intensity of hardship's attachment to the polytheist human, to the extent that it is as though he was created in hardship.

The meaning is: We created hardship within the disbelieving human.

The commentators have other interpretations of the meaning of the verse, which the context does not support.

This sentence is a *badal al-ishtimal* (a substitute that is connected to the preceding phrase through an implied link) for the sentence, ﴿We have indeed created man in toil﴾ [al-Balad: 4].

The interrogative form is used to rebuke and to show that the person is mistaken.

The pronoun in *ayahsibu* ("does he think") necessarily refers to man. Among the effects of the perplexity over the meaning of ﴿We have indeed created man in toil﴾ [al-Balad: 4] is that some exegetes took the pronoun in *ayahsibu* to refer to a particular individual covered by the word "man", such as Abu al-Ashudd al-Jumahi. This is adding one confusion upon another.

[Page 353]

They follow the blameworthy traits of his character with the blameworthy things he says: false boasting, and praising himself for squandering wealth without any good purpose. The people of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance) used to brag about squandering wealth and regarded it as a virtue, since it indicated that the owner cared little for it. 'Antarah said:

*When I am drunk, I squander my wealth, and my honour remains whole and unblemished.*

*And when I am sober, I do not fall short in generosity, as you know of my character and my nobility.*

The clause ﴿يَقُولُ أهْلَكْتُ مالًا﴾ ("He says: I have squandered wealth in abundance") is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to "al-insān" (the human being). This is from the affliction (kabad).

The clause ﴿أيَحْسَبُ أنْ لَمْ يَرَهُ أحَدٌ﴾ ("Does he think that no one sees him?") is a comprehensive substitute (badal al-ishtimal) for the clause ﴿يَقُولُ أهْلَكْتُ مالًا﴾, because his statement ﴿أهْلَكْتُ مالًا لُبَدًا﴾ is uttered while he thinks that his lie has been accepted by all people, whereas there are always some people who become aware of his lie. Zuhayr said:

*Whatever disposition a man may have, even if he thinks it hidden from people, it will become known.*

The interrogative form expresses denial and rebuke, and it is a metonymy (kināyah) for God's knowledge of his inner nature and for the fact that his boasting of generosity is false.

*Lubadan* is read with a *ḍamma* on the *lām* and a *fatḥa* on the *bā'* in the recitation of the majority of readers. It is the plural of *lubdah* (with a *ḍamma* on the *lām*), which denotes what has become matted of wool or hair, that is, what has gathered and whose parts have stuck together. Abu Ja'far read it as *lubbadan*, with a *ḍamma* on the *lām* and a *shaddah* on the *bā'*, either as the plural of *lābid* in the sense of "gathered, one part joined to another," like *ṣayyam* and *qayyam*, or as a noun on the pattern *fa''al*, like *zummal* (for a coward) and *jubba'* (for a weak person).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 90, verses 8–10:

(﴿Did We not make for him two eyes?﴾ ﴿And a tongue and two lips?﴾ ﴿And guide him to the two highways?﴾)

This is a justification (ta'lil) for the denunciation and rebuke in His saying: (﴿Does he think that no one has power over him?﴾ [al-Balad: 5]) or His saying: (﴿Does he think that no one has seen him?﴾ [al-Balad: 7]). That is: he is heedless of the power of God Most High and of His all-encompassing knowledge of all beings, which is indicated by the fact that He created the organs of perception, among which are the two eyes, and created the instruments of expression, which are the tongue and the two lips. How, then, could the One who bestows knowledge upon people be unable to act or be unaware of their conditions? God Most High says: (﴿Should not He who created know? And He is the Subtle, the Acquainted.﴾ [al-Mulk: 14]).

The interrogative may be affirmative in meaning (taqriri) or denunciatory (inkari).

Page 354
The singling out of the two eyes is because they are the most beneficial of the organs of perception, and because what is being refuted is his supposition that no one has seen him. The mention of the two lips along with the tongue is because expression is achieved through both together: the tongue does not articulate without the two lips, and the two lips do not articulate without the tongue.

Among the subtleties of the Qur'an is that it did not limit itself to the tongue alone nor to the two lips alone, contrary to the Arabs' habit of limiting themselves to one of them. They say: "He speaks with an eloquent tongue," and they say: "He did not speak a word (lit. with the tip of a lip)," or "he did not utter a sound with the tip of a lip." This is because the context is one of argument (istidlal), so there is mentioned that which gives greater depiction of the creation of the organ of speech.

Having mentioned that by which knowledge is acquired and that by which things known are expressed, He followed with what guides thought to reflection and inquiry, and that is His saying: (﴿And guide him to the two highways﴾).

Thus the discourse completes the principles of learning and teaching: man was created loving knowledge and loving to make himself known. By the organs of perception he acquires observations, which are the roots of certain knowledge; by speech he conveys what he teaches to others; and by guidance to good and evil he distinguishes between his knowledge and refines it.

The two lips are the two fleshy parts that cover the mouth and its teeth, and by them one sucks water. By their opening and closing the sounds of the letters through which speech is produced are shaped, and this is what is intended here.

The root of shafah (lip) is shafw, from which the waw was dropped and a ha' was substituted for it, so its plural is shafawat. It has also been said that its root is shafah with a ha' that is the final radical of the word, and the feminine ha' was substituted for it, so its plural is shafahat and shifah. What appears to be the case is that the original is shafah with an original ha', then the ha' was treated like the feminine ha' for lightening in pause, so they said shafah, and through frequent use this was forgotten, so it was treated like the feminine ha', as in the verse. This is what its dual requires, shafatayn, rather than their saying shafawayn, for they agreed that the dual returns the noun to its original form.

Guidance (hidayah) is indicating the path that conveys one to the intended place toward which one travels.

The najd is raised land, elevated but less than a mountain. So what is meant here is two elevated roads (najdan), and a road may be ascending and uphill, or a low-lying valley.

Page 355
Guidance is here metaphorically applied to the inspiration God placed in man, by which he perceives what harms and what benefits, and this is the basis of human civilization and the basis of sciences; and guidance by the religion of Islam is to that in which success lies.

The two najds are used metaphorically for good and evil, and they are called two najds because following one of them, which is good, is difficult, so it is given precedence over the two paths; or because each of them is difficult in some respect: the path of good is difficult in traversing it, and the path of evil is difficult in its consequences. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 90, verses 11–17 (part 2 of 2):

Whoever takes *thumma* (ثُمَّ, "then") to denote a delay in time, the meaning becomes: "He did not storm the steep path, and then followed it with faith." That is, he stormed the steep path in the Jahiliyyah (the period of ignorance before Islam) and then embraced Islam when Islam came.

This is stated explicitly in the hadith of Hakim ibn Hizam in the Sahih. He said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, have you seen the things I used to do *tahannuth* (تَحَنُّث) in the Jahiliyyah, such as charity, manumission, and maintaining ties of kinship? The meaning is that his entry into Islam brought him reward for his deeds, as if he had done them within Islam.

He said *"min alladhina amanu"* (مِنَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا, "of those who believed") rather than "then he was a believer," because being "of those who believed" is a stronger indication of the establishment of faith than describing him as "a believer." Enjoining one another to compassion is a great virtue. It is also an allusion to their being characterised by compassion, because whoever enjoins compassion is one who knows its worth and excellence, so he practises it before he enjoins it, as mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿and you do not urge one another to feed the poor﴾ [al-Fajr 89:18].

This is stated explicitly in His words: ﴿And who is better in speech than one who invites to Allah, does righteous deeds, and says, "Indeed, I am of the Muslims"﴾ [Fussilat 41:33], up to His words: ﴿But none is granted it except those who are patient﴾ [Fussilat 41:35], and His words: ﴿Rather, you do not honour the orphan﴾ [al-Fajr 89:17] ﴿and you do not urge one another to feed the poor﴾ [al-Fajr 89:18].

When he had praised those who believed, he followed the praise and the good tidings for them by opening with the demonstrative pronoun, to distinguish them in the most complete way, because it brings their attributes to the mind of the listener, along with what the demonstrative pronoun carries of intending honour and exaltation.

*Al-maymana* means the direction of the right. It is a *maf'ala* noun of place, derived from the verb *yamana* (in the past tense), meaning that something was on his right, that is, on the side of his right hand. Alternatively, it is derived from *yamanahu Allah yumnan*, meaning that God blessed him. Either of the two roots is derived from the other. It has been said that the right hand was called *yamin* and *yumna* because it is more beneficial to its owner in the ease of his affairs. For the same reason, the land of Yemen was called *Yaman*, because it lies on the right side of one who stands facing the Ka'ba from its door. The door of the Ka'ba faces east, so the direction on the right of one who enters the Ka'ba is the south, and that is the direction of the land of Yemen. The land of Yemen was famous for its bounties, so it is *maymuna* (blessed). The Greek geographers used to describe it in Arabic as "the Happy Arabia." From this there arose the belief, among the people of augury and omen-reading, that what comes from the right, of wild animals and birds, is a bearer of good news. Hence the phrase "the blessed right-sides." Al-Muraqqish refuted this belief, saying:

*So the ill-omened are like the right-sided, and the right-sided are like the ill-omened.*

From the opposite belief there arose the naming of the land of Sham as *Sha'm*, with a hamza, derived from *shu'm* (ill omen), because the land of Sham lies to the north of one who enters the Ka'ba. Islam nullified this belief by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Allah, bless us in our Sham and in our Yemen." Their naming of the opposite of the right hand as the left (*yasar*) was only to nullify what was imagined of ill omen in it.

Since the right side was an honoured side, they customarily sat on the right in gatherings, as a mark of honour for the one seated there, and they made the opposite of that for the other. Islam nullified this, so people would sit wherever the gathering ended for them.

The companions of Paradise were called the companions of the right hand (*maymana*) and the companions of the right (*yamin*). The people of Hell were called "the companions of the left hand" (*mash'ama*) and "the companions of the left" (*shimal*) in Surat al-Waqi'a. So His saying, ﴿Those are the companions of the right hand﴾, means: those are the companions of honour with God.

[Page 363]

His saying, ﴿they are the companions of the left hand﴾, means: they are the despised. This is a metonymy (*kinaya*), based on the custom of the Arabs at that time in their gatherings. There is no literal right side or left side here, since the literal meaning of *maymana* and *mash'ama* requires a space for the one to whom the direction is attributed.

The clause ﴿But those who disbelieved in Our signs, they are the companions of the left hand﴾ completes what was said of the blameworthy human being mentioned just before. His blame was not followed there by its threat, out of concern for what is more important, which is the mention of the state of his opposites and their promise. When that matter had been fulfilled, the reins were turned back to that human being. From this wondrous arrangement there results the rhetorical device of *radd al-'ajuz 'ala al-sadr* (repeating the end of a phrase at the beginning), and the rhetorical device of antithesis (*tibaq*) between *maymana* and *mash'ama*.

You have already learned that *mash'ama* is the station of humiliation and wrath, and for that reason it is followed by His saying: ﴿Over them will be a fire sealed shut﴾.

The pronoun of separation (*damir al-fasl*) in His saying ﴿they are the companions of the left hand﴾ is for strengthening the judgement, and it is not for restriction (*qasr*), since restriction has already been obtained from the mention of the clause opposed to the one before it, which is ﴿Those are the companions of the right hand﴾.

*Muwsada* is a passive participle from *awsada al-bab* (he closed the door) with a waw. It is also said *a'sada*, with a hamza, and both are two dialects. It has been said that the hamza is the dialect of Quraysh. It has also been said that its meaning is: he made it a *wasida*. The *wasida* is a dwelling made of stones in the mountains for guarding camels. The majority read *muwsada* with a silent waw after the mim, from *awsada*. Abu 'Amr, Hamza, Hafs on the authority of 'Asim, Ya'qub and Khalaf read it with a silent hamza after the mim, from *a'sada al-bab*, with two hamzas, meaning *wasadahu* (he closed it).

*'Alayhim* (over them) is connected to *muwsada* (sealed shut). It was placed before its governing word to give importance to the attachment of the locking upon them, hastening the instilling of dread.

With this placement, the rhyme with the *ha'* sound has been established, beginning from His saying: ﴿But he has not attempted the steep path﴾ [al-Balad: 11].

[Page 364]

The attribution of being sealed shut to the fire is a rational metaphor (*majaz 'aqli*), and what is sealed shut is the place of the fire, that is, Hell.
